item.description:
Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Bertie's witcher skills are a bit rusty; Dom goes through the Gears; Kelsey enjoys a horror game that feels just like home; and Chris does an incredible impression of a butler that no one acknowledged.
But enough of that: what have you been playing this week?
And don't forget we have an entire dusty archive of previous What We've Been Playings, just in case you don't trust your memory any more and want to check which games you've played and see what you thought of them.
It's weird returning to a game I think I know really well only to discover I don't really know it that well any more at all. The familiarity slowly dribbles back and broad strokes of the game I can of course remember, but that muscle memory that was once so readily there has gone. I bumbled around like an idiot in The Witcher 3 for a couple of hours when revisiting it for the Remastered release this week. I felt like Roach stranded on a rooftop.
I compared the game a lot to The Blood of Dawnwalker while I played, too, which isn't a surprise given how similar they are, and in how they're directed by the same person, Konrad Tomaszkiewicz (and made by many of the same people). And stood side by side, The Witcher 3 holds up remarkably well, which is impressive given that it's now 11 years old.
Indeed, The Witcher 3 even outdoes Dawnwalker in some regards (perhaps many regards). One particular example is the city of Novigrad and its size and interactivity, and the sheer number of people bumbling around, swearing at you. It's a place like few others I've experienced in a role-playing game, and I've said it before and I'll say it again: that's one of gaming's great cities, that is.
Let's see what GTA 6 says when it comes out in November, eh?
I've been reviewing this game for the past week, and it's taken me a much larger chunk of time than I thought it would to grit my teeth and push through the Hardcore difficulty than I thought - there's at least 20 hours of game in the campaign alone if you're playing on any of the more advanced difficulties. I'll be staying on the game to test out Horde and PvP in the coming days (God, I hope my old-person reflexes don't humiliate me too much), and I am not upset about that prospect, either. It's nice to have a game that focuses this much on catharsis and release when the industry is in such dire straits.
I unfortunately haven't had much time or energy to play anything this week that isn't embargoed, but I did make time to watch Jacksepticeye's playthrough of Silent Hill: Townfall with my housemate after playing it myself a few weeks ago and damn, what a game! It also definitely helps that Townfall is where my favourite in-game place - Silent Hill - and my home, the UK, have finally managed to collide. I might be a little biased in that regard, but still, if you like Silent Hill in any shape or form, play it!
It still feels surreal that Konami has not only revived Silent Hill as an IP, but has managed to do it with real style and fervour. Silent Hill 2 Remake has a special place in my heart of course, and Silent Hill f was pretty good - soulslite combat aside - but the publisher has really nailed things with Silent HillL Townfall, and I am so excited to see Screen Burn hopefully get a lot more attention off the back of this.
I managed to achieve the fabled both-parents-go-out-child-free moment for the first time in an age this past weekend, for a nice low-key gathering around a friend's. We were supposed to bring something to play (not a video game, obviously; something a normal person might bring with them to play) as well as a dish, but everybody forgot, so we ended up with a lot of desserts and not a lot to do afterwards for a quick laugh.
Heads Up! became the solution and it was, frankly, better than any new or clever or convoluted game, video or otherwise that I could've dug up to bring around myself. If you're unfamiliar, it's essentially Articlate! (which is basically Pictionary but with talking instead of drawing). Nobody kept score, everyone kept flicking up on the phone to pass and down to mark the answer correct, when it's really the other way round (or is it?! I don't even know myself), and even in these entirely non-competitive circumstances I found it very hard not to get annoyed at someone not immediately recognising my note-perfect impression for the word "Butler". Anyway! Sometimes the classics are the best.

item.title: GTA 6 is seemingly adding another naughty pastime to the series' already mammoth collection of naughty pastimes. Joining the strip clubs and violent car-jackings and carefree murder is "frequent and prominent" drug use that you can try "at any time," according to a new age rating. Read more
item.description:
GTA 6 is seemingly adding another naughty pastime to the series' already mammoth collection of naughty pastimes. Joining the strip clubs and violent car-jackings and carefree murder is "frequent and prominent" drug use that you can try "at any time," according to a new age rating.
Grand Theft Auto 6 recently received a PEGI 18+ age rating that was uploaded and then quickly deleted from the Pan European Game Information board's website, but not before fans saved and then shared details from the listing.
Most of PEGI's description covers what you'd expect from a Grand Theft Auto game. There's murder, robberies, gun crime, other illegal shenanigans and lots of swears. What's new in this sixth numbered GTA is the free usage of hard drugs, apparently.
"Drug use is frequent and prominent with the player being able to partake in drug use with others and to use illegal drugs directly from their inventory," the now-deleted rating stated. "Most notably, cocaine can be carried around by the player and snorted directly from their hand at any time."
While most GTA stories usually centre drug trade in some fashion, most of the series' protagonists aren't so enthusiastic about using the goods they sell. GTA 5 and GTA Online both include optional bongs, sure, but they can normally only be found in player-owned apartments, not carried about in the wider world.
A separate age rating from earlier today suggested that GTA 6 may be the first Grand Theft Auto game to directly depict sex scenes, and the PEGI listing corroborates that info too: "There are also strong sexual themes, including nudity, scenes of intercourse and occasional scenes of sexual fetishes. In various night clubs the player can also pay for private dances, during which, the game allows the player to move their hands onto the dancers' breasts and buttocks."
And, finally, there's the unsurprising presence of violence, as is the norm for Rockstar Games. PEGI said players can "harm all other characters inhabiting the environment" with a "high degree of realism." Some weapons will obviously "cause greater damage such as detailed decapitation and dismemberment."
Rockstar devs have been boasting about how they've significantly upped the detail in GTA 6's "re-engineered" weather system and in, well, every other corner of the game, so more realistic violence is probably unsurprising, especially given the series' history.

item.title: Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden has some thoughts on where Team Xbox is at right now and where the green machine can go from here, but the console maker needs to "pick a lane" with exclusive games, either way. Read more
item.description:
Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden has some thoughts on where Team Xbox is at right now and where the green machine can go from here, but the console maker needs to "pick a lane" with exclusive games, either way.
As Xbox Series X/S console sales continued to decline this generation, the company flip-flopped quite a few times when it came to its first-party exclusives. Microsoft went from releasing almost all of its games exclusively on PC and Xbox consoles to becoming a sort-of third-party publisher during Phil Spencer's tenure as head of Xbox - everything from Starfield to Halo: Campaign Evolved found their way to PS5.
In a chat with The Expansion Pass podcast (embedded below), Layden said most of Xbox's current woes come from the company's inability to commit to exclusives. "Or if they picked a lane, they didn't stay in it very long," he said. "Are you going to be a platform? A platform needs exclusives or else the platform has no meaning. Or are you going to be the biggest publisher in the world now that you have Activision and Blizzard? And if you're the biggest publisher in the world, you almost have to be on every platform because that's how the business model works. You can't be successful at both."
Layden did acknowledge that current Xbox CEO Asha Sharma seems to be trying to "right the ship" in recent months. "I hope she does it, though I don't know what that looks like." Since her appointment at the start of the year, Sharma kicked off a corporate restructure that'll result in 3,200 lost jobs when all is said and done. She also signed Hideo Kojima's Physint and bought back some console exclusives with Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution.
"This is your Dreamcast moment," Layden continued, referring to when Sega abandoned its final console and decided to become a prominent publisher on its competitor's systems. "It can be done. It's been done before. So, that's my advice. Pick a lane."
Sharma recently shot down speculation about Microsoft selling Xbox, and said she wants to course correct "whatever it takes." So far, the company's so-called reset seems geared toward supporting its biggest franchises - your Elder Scrolls, Halos, Fallouts and Call of Duties. The next-gen Project Helix sounds like it's still going ahead, too.

item.title: Warhorse Studios co-founder Martin Klima - the developer behind last year's historical RPG Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 - is crossing his fingers for higher game prices, and he thinks GTA 6 might be the one to usher in a new normal. Read more
item.description:
Warhorse Studios co-founder Martin Klima - the developer behind last year's historical RPG Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 - is crossing his fingers for higher game prices, and he thinks GTA 6 might be the one to usher in a new normal.
Speaking to PC Gamer in a recent interview, the studio boss explained that the games industry is facing a few major problems. The cost of game development has ballooned wildly in recent years, but the audience that regularly buys new games has somewhat peaked. On top of that, the move to digital storefronts means the middle-man of retail is more or less cut out: "We destroyed retail, and we took all their money."
So, how else can studios maximise cash flow without stuffing games full of microtransactions? "The last thing you can do is to increase the unit price," Klima said. "That would help a lot, but everybody's scared to death about it. Now, hopefully, GTA will blaze the trail, and it will allow us to increase the cost."
According to Klima, Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two are the last ones "who can afford, or who can dare, to increase the price of games, which I think is long overdue and also necessary for this business to survive. So I wish them all the luck."
GTA 6 is priced similarly to many other high-end triple-A games here in the UK - the Standard Edition costs £69.99. Across the pond in the US, however, GTA 6's Standard Edition sells for $79.99, about $10 more expensive than most blockbuster games not called Mario Kart World. The Ultimate Edition can go up to $99.99.
The next Grand Theft Auto will likely be the biggest game launch of all time, despite the higher costs in some territories, but there's no guarantee players will accept an $80 price tag for any game. Case in point, last year, Xbox tried to launch The Outer Worlds 2 for $80 before having to back peddle and sell the sci-fi satire for the usual $70.
Although Klima's rooting for Rockstar's success, he's not all too interested in the upcoming crime romp either way. "I am not going to be playing GTA 6 unless I'm somehow forced to," he added. "And the reason why it is so popular - it beats me. It's something which I just fail to understand." Regardless, he's still happy that "somebody is making these games that are really technologically marvels."
Grand Theft Auto 6 comes to PS5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19 November. Just earlier today, we learned the game might be the first GTA to feature full-on sex scenes. At the same time, developer Rockstar is in the middle of an employment tribunal in Scotland after being accused of union-busting by a group of fired workers.

item.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 may feature actual sex scenes. The suggestion comes from an age-rating description for GTA 6 on the PlayStation Store, which states - if viewing the New Zealand or Australian versions of the Store - there are "sex scenes" in the game. Read more
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto 6 may feature actual sex scenes. The suggestion comes from an age-rating description for GTA 6 on the PlayStation Store, which states - if viewing the New Zealand or Australian versions of the Store - there are "sex scenes" in the game.
Should this be true, it could make GTA 6 the first Grand Theft Auto game to directly feature sexual intercourse. To feature it on purpose, that is; you might remember the infamous Hot Coffee scandal that surrounded GTA: San Andreas. A mod reinstated a sex mini-game Rockstar pulled out of San Andreas before release, causing all sorts of problems for the company.
Since then, GTA has featured risqué dalliances with sex workers in GTA games, involving some degree of nudity, but most actual sex scenes have happened off camera. There was that sex scene in GTA 4 expansion pack The Ballad of Gay Tony, but it only gave a brief glimpse at two characters humping with their clothes mostly on. There have been various depictions of oral sex, but again, they've been mostly obscured.
However, these age-rating descriptions - spotted by IGN - may not be accurate. They're not separately searchable on the relevant age-ratings boards' websites, despite the ESRB, PEGI and Australian Ratings Board's logos appearing on the PlayStation Store. Presumably this has something to do with embargoed information when posting fuller listings.
Even if they are accurate, a mention of "sex scenes" doesn't necessarily mean fully featured sex, though the UK version of the PS Store listing does mention "sexual content" and displays a symbol for "sex". That symbol is also attached to games like Baldur's Gate 3 and Cyberpunk 2077, which have fairly graphic sex scenes. Indeed, the PEGI "sex" symbol being there - whereas it isn't attached to The Blood of Dawnwalker, a game that features partial nudity and sexual content - does suggest there's something stronger here.
Is it a surprise? GTA 6 is a story about a couple - Jason and Lucia - which certainly lends credibility to the existence of sex scenes, particularly when we know that their romantic connection is a central part of the game, and as we've seen what looks like the beginnings of a sex scene in an official GTA 6 trailer (jump to one minute 12 seconds).
Also, since GTA 5 came out in 2013, intimate scenes have become a lot more commonplace. There are several in GTA-like open-world RPG Cyberpunk 2077, and in Baldur's Gate 3, and there are some in The Blood of Dawnwalker, to name but a few. For GTA 6 to feature a graphic sex scene would hardly be provocative in this day and age.
Grand Theft Auto 6 releases 19th November. There's been a deluge of information released about GTA 6 in recent weeks, after an Extended Look trailer aired on Netflix, and after footage was leaked by hackers in the lead up to it. Meanwhile, Rockstar is battling an employment tribunal in Scotland related to the sudden removal of 31 employees last year, which it declares was done for confidentiality breaching reasons, but the former employees allege was union-busting.

item.description:
We recently learned that Microsoft gave development of its next Halo game to Activision, where "a new purpose-built team" - separate from the teams working on Call of Duty - has been created to oversee the franchise going forward. Now, in a report from well-known Halo and Xbox insider Rebs Gaming, a possible timeline about how the process progressed internally at Microsoft has started to take form. And the report suggests that Activision's take on Xbox's premiere sci-fi shooter will be a reboot of the series -one that possibly explores Master Chief's origins.
"Activision originally proposed two separate games: a free to play multiplayer game and a campaign-only game," Rebs Gaming said in the video. "I'm told Activision's original idea for the campaign-only game prototype was a soft reboot that doesn't follow Halo Infinite's story but doesn't retcon any previously established canon." But Activision apparently mooted the idea of making two separate games - a multiplayer and single-player offering - instead opting to go for one package combining both elements, more in line with what we've seen from the Halo series to date.
If you're not a fan of the Halo novels, the closest we've come to a Master Chief origin story was in the slightly pants Halo Paramount Halo TV show, which was cancelled after two seasons. You have to wonder, if Activision does go back in time to show the ultra-fascist roots of Master Chief's rebellion-crushing origins, will he also have sex in front of Cortana in the game? Probably not, ey.
Rebs also noted that teams at Sledgehammer Games have already "conceptualised and prototyped basic gameplay mechanics for both the proposed campaign and multiplayer projects", and pitched ideas around player movement. This has apparently all taken place within the Infinity Ward Engine, proprietary tech that has been the backbone of Call of Duty games, in some way, as far back as Call of Duty 2 in 2005. The modern version of the engine was completely rebuilt in 2019 for Modern Warfare, and is a pretty solid bit of tech - thanks to how modern games look, we know it can handle path tracing and ray tracing very well. This means that Activision is potentially moving away from Unreal Engine 5 (used in Campaign Evolved) and that Halo Studios' expensive, proprietary Slipstream engine is now completely dead.
In the report, Rebs suggested that the overall team that'll take ownership of the new title may well be built "within Sledgehammer Games", per the report. "Please keep in mind that Activision's Halo project is in early development so things can change," Rebs warned.. And yes, we should take all this news speculatively: the only thing Activision has confirmed for sure is that it will be developing the next Halo title.
Halo: Campaign Evolved launched to strong reviews recently - I thought it was a great, if not perfect, mulligan of a classic - though its sales seemed to lack the punch Xbox wanted (even if it did net $67 million in gross revenue within its first two weeks). But Halo is still a tentpole brand for Microsoft and Xbox. However, Xbox is still currently undergoing major reorganisation, with the recent Halo stewardship change resulting in major layoffs at Halo Studios, which has all but closed, and at other studios in the Xbox division.

item.description:
A few years ago, I had the chance to ask Alex Ward, the co-founder of Criterion Games, about the driving model for the Burnout series. I had heard from a friend that beneath the arcadey immediacy lay physics of rare nuance and beauty. I was reverent in my questioning, even if I was slightly clueless - is it a driving model or a handling model or a physics model? - and Ward, thankfully, was having none of it. He told me that in the very early Burnout games, the cars, such as they were, didn't actually have wheels. How's that for nuance.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer, then, with its landspeeders and podracers, all of them ghosting over the ground on some kind of blurry antigrav cushion, is a kind of homecoming. Ward may not be involved, but Fuse Games, the developer, has an awful lot of Criterion DNA coiled up inside it. If you're like me, and you've come to accept the fact, over the years, that Burnout 3 and Burnout Paradise are, together, the most thrilling video games ever made, that's a good thing. But even if you know nothing at all about Burnout, you're going to have a very pleasant time here.
I'm starting with Burnout rather than Star Wars because I feel like Galactic Racer does that too. Sure there's some lovely faux-Williams music to kick us off, twinkly and intriguing out in space, martial and brooding down on the planets, and we're wedged somewhere in the timeline between Episode 6 and Episode 7. There are droids and desert planets and fish-headed aliens. But the game came alive for me in my first race, on my first corner, when I realised that if I was playing Burnout, I would press a particular face button right about now to ignite boost for the first time. Purely running on muscle memory I pushed the button while the thought was occurring to me. And I got the same boost. The same feeling. I was jolted back in my chair. Speed, yes, but the horizon seemed to broaden and shimmer. I was home.
A dozen little similarities followed over those first races. The crash cam, when you knock someone else off the road, still swoops backwards to catch the tumbling wreckage and then rushes forward to catch up with you as it did in Burnout 3. There may be no wheels involved, but there's still a grippy sense (if slightly diminished, as is, just slightly, the sense of weight) that pulls you to the ground and seems to hold you there, the center of gravity in the very middle of your speeding machine. Takedowns are still called Takedowns! Boost indulged at the right moment can still change everything. You are still encouraged - and I will put this delicately - to drive like a deeply mean-spirited son of a bitch. This is not a game for polite daytime racers. It wants you to grit your teeth so hard that they start to turn to dust.
All of this is a wonderful basis for a Star Wars game, it turns out, and this is where we actually get to the Galaxy Far Far Away. Burnout slots into this universe so well because the take on Star Wars that Fuse is pursuing is the junky/formidable technology side. Forget Jedis and wookies and midiclorians, a word I am only slightly surprised to discover that Google cannot autocorrect, so knock yourself out. Forget all that stuff. This is the Star Wars of the Millennium Falcon, which needs to be thumped just so before its engines start, and which is a thing of switches and buttons and which shudders dangerously when it drops out of hyperspace. It's the Star Wars of landcraft that's fast as heck but rusty and looks like the back panel of a refrigerator. It's the Star Wars of malfunctioning droids that shower sparks and squeal and are always ready to throw off loose parts.
The extent to which Galactic Racer delivers this sense of brilliant, decrepit, nearly ruined technology is astonishing. And I can't really tell you about it in one go, because it gets right to the heart of all the different pieces that make this game work.
So take boosting. This is a little piece of genius, I think: Galactic Racer has not one boost but two. The first is called Afterburner and it feels a lot like Burnout's boost. Hold down a button and you go like heck until the boost bar is drained. (At which point, unlike Burnout, it will generally refill on its own.) This boost is fun and in any other game it might even be overpowered. But in Galactic Racer it's... it's fine. In Galactic Racer, it's the safe option.
And this is because of the other boost, which is known as the Ramjet. This boost is much faster, and when it charges up you have to switch over to it with a stab of a thumbstick. This here is what I'm talking about in terms of the game's delivery of brilliantly terrible technology. There is this thump and shudder when you switch over from Afterburner to Ramject that suggests somewhere in the dark spaces of your rattling craft, mechanical things are moving about and realigning themselves. That sound effect alone is just magic.
But that's just the sound effect! They great thing about Ramjet is it's a better boost than Afterburner but it's also dangerous. Leave it on too long and you get in to a section of the boost bar that's known as redlining. An alarm starts to sound - the same alarm I often hear when I'm in dreams in which I have to pilot a 747 and I don't know what any of the buttons do - and then, give it long enough, and you explode.
To boost or not to boost, then? That was the eternal Burnout conundrum. Now it's to boost or to boost in a way that might kill you? And it's all channeled through the experience of driving these wonderfully clanky metal beasts around at high speeds.
Two boosts suggests a layer of strategy to the racing, and it's here we probably need to get at the game's main conceit. I've delayed it a little, but in truth, I spent a pleasant hour enjoying this return to Burnout-land without noticing it myself. Anyway: Galactic Racer's campaign is a Roguelite.
And even this is all about the tech. You pick between one of three craft types, from dependable Landspeeders to darting, bad-at-corners, Speederbikes and Skim Speeders, the royalty of the race track that can turn on their sides for extra manoeuvrability but also come with a bit of a learning curve. Pick one of these guys and then you're off into a series of races split across a series of acts but also a series of planets. You make decisions on what event to select next via one of those FTL-style branching path maps that are everywhere these days.
Decisions! You choose between races, elimination races, story-based encounters with other racers, and even chances to take a bespoke craft out for a special event. All the while you're trying to earn enough money from each race to kit out your vehicle and make it as fast and as powerful as it can so that you can finish first in the final race of the act and move forward. And yes, if you lose that final race - or if you crash out in an eliminator - you go back to the start with all those additions to your machine lost. (Although being a Roguelite rather than a Roguelike, your starting machines do get better over time.)
Into this structure, the game pours an awful lot of stuff, more than enough to make each run feel unique. You're racing against a set cast of other racers, but your relationships with them may change from one playthrough to the next depending on whether you make deals with them, swap parts with them or develop rivalries. But more importantly there's the stuff you do to your craft. Each race leaves you with cash to buy new parts, as well as core upgrades to your machine's basic stats, and perhaps even new abilities that work a little like the kinds of things you might get in Mario Kart. Maybe you want mines to drop on the field. Maybe you want a burst of auto pilot. Maybe you want to do something nasty to others when you crash.
The best way to talk about the interaction of all of this stuff - parts and abilities and upgrades - is to tell you that in my last run, I put all my points into two stats: one measuring how robust my craft was when it came to running into walls, and another that measured how much Afterburner I had. I ignored everything else - my Ramjet, my cornering abilities, all that crucial jazz. And I did this because I was picking parts that extended my Afterburner and also extended how fast it recharged. And then I doubled down on abilities that granted me autopilot. By the time I had reached the final races, I was almost always boosting, and I was simultaneously almost never doing any actual steering. I had hacked together a deeply unwise build and I was utterly committed to it. (Sadly it eroded my skills to the point that when I had to start over without autopilot I just rammed into walls endlessly.)
Add to all this Racer Styles that foreground different approaches and Favours, which act as selectable load-outs of perks, and you have a Roguelite with a surprising range of variables. Don't take what I've just said above and mark this down as the game where you can just rely on autopilot, by the bye. You can play through the game for hours without touching autopilot. But if you're a weirdo, you can find some wonderfully weird ways to play this game.
This stuff, as is the way of Roguelites, is both dizzyingly complex and utterly simple. Parts, Racer Styles, Favours etc: they're all good things that might happen to you. And out on the race track there are bad things that might happen to you too. If you sustain damage and you fumble recovery, you will lose one of your parts and you'll have to work without that 25 percent boost, say, until you get it fixed in between planets. Maybe you fall out with a rival in a story encounter and then the next time you start a race - there's a wonderful bit of business where you tap in codes to bring each of your machine's systems online early, and it feels just like flicking overhead switches in an X-Wing - rather than zipping into the distance, you just explode. You just explode.
Luckily, Galactic Racer never forgets that between the loot and the loadout and the story choices this is still a racing game. And with that we're back to Burnout - and back to Star Wars, somehow. The game has that ceaseless full-ahead pelt that Burnout offers and each corner is a set-piece, even before you tip your Skim Speeder onto one edge. But different planets don't just have their own looks, they have their own impacts. Icy worlds make your Ramjet cooler and longer-lasting. Toxic worlds will corrode you if you spend too long racing over lakes of lurid acid. Desert worlds will bake you to the point where it might be worth leaving the Ramjet off as much as possible. Your call.
These worlds don't just look beautiful, from Jakku's dunes and wrecked Star Destroyers you must thread between to Crait's white crystalline surface with red dust billowing underneath. They're also carved up into fascinating tracks that blend tight underground corridors where cornering is a constant discussion with death, and daringly wide-open outside sections where I once got so turned around I ended up going backwards. These are places that constantly shift in the way that they challenge you, and I suspect that better racers than me will spend an awfully long time working out the optimal strategies for handling each one.
All of that and it's Star Wars, down to the Droids passing by in the on-foot sections between races where you visit the shop and chat to your rivals, and down to the glimpse of a very familiar targeting computer I saw on the dashboard of a new craft I just unlocked. Down even to the wonderful array of English regional accents that suggest dayplayers doing their bits at Elstree Studios. And it's also a lovely suite of racing options, with arcade modes and a suite of themed mini-tours and multiplayer one-offs and multiplayer micro-campaigns, and even a little Pod Racing thrown in. It's new games, with Roguelite choices and endless unlockables, and it's also old games, with cruel and ingenious courses where everything can be lost in an instant. It's a Galaxy Far, Far Away, and it's also Paradise City.
A copy of Star Wars: Galactic Racer was provided for this review by Secret Mode.

item.title: Gears of War: E-Day arrived for early adopters yesterday, available for anyone who bought either the Premium Edition, Premium Upgrade Edition, or Collector's Edition version of the game. As it arrived, however, some players noted 'missing' features that have appeared in past Gears games, but not in The Coalition's latest. Read more
item.description:
Gears of War: E-Day arrived for early adopters yesterday, available for anyone who bought either the Premium Edition, Premium Upgrade Edition, or Collector's Edition version of the game. As it arrived, however, some players noted 'missing' features that have appeared in past Gears games, but not in The Coalition's latest.
In a statement timed with the launch of the game, the studio noted that these 'legacy features' - such as Meat Shields, Chainsaw Duels, select weapons from the franchise’s past, and Private Lobbies and leaderboards - may arrive either post-launch or "in [The Coalition's] next title".
"We started E-Day with an empty hard drive building our entire gameplay sandbox from scratch to ensure a more unified gameplay experience across Campaign, PvE and PvP," the studio said. "This new sandbox also allowed for innovation in cover, combat and enemies. The trade-off being that including every legacy feature from Gears of War was not possible for launch.
"Those features, like Meat Shields, Chainsaw Duels, select weapons from the franchise’s past, and online work like Private Lobbies and leaderboards – are not gone from the franchise. Our team is working hard to deliver the strongest and most stable launch experience we can with an eye to how, and what, to deliver and improve on fan-favourite features either post-launch or in our next title."
Interesting. Given the mood at The Coalition and the very public, very controversial cuts that Microsoft is making across the Xbox division, it's striking to hear a developer talk about 'next titles'. Part of the most recent wave of layoffs saw E-Day's story director, Juan Vaca, depart the studio, which means if there is a sequel, it will presumably feel different.. I praised the story and campaign quite a lot in my Gears of War: E-Day review.
Other points outlined in the studio's post revolved around the Gnasher shotgun. "The Gnasher is one of the most iconic and unique weapons in Gears of War," the studio said, "we believe it always needs to be punchy, visceral and consistent every time you pull the trigger. As many fans know, the way aiming and firing works has evolved over time, but these goals never change. Every Gears game has fired the Gnasher from the camera position when aiming with the left trigger. This results in an accurate and predictable shot from the ADS view – this is not changed in E-Day." There's a lot of description about the changes the studio is making to how aiming works with the gun, but the long and short of it is: The Coalition is expecting feedback on it, and will listen to what players have to say.
E-Day's first Season kicked off with the Early Access release yesterday and will be live for eight weeks, ending on 1st December. Ranked modes for PvP arrive on 13th October. The game sees a general release on 6th October - and E-Day appears to already be doing well on Steam and Xbox. Let's hope a general release gives it even more of a push.

item.title: AI image upscaling is coming to PlayStation 5, Sony has announced, and it's available already in two games: Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei. Read more
item.description:
AI image upscaling is coming to PlayStation 5, Sony has announced, and it's available already in two games: Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei.
The image-upscaling technology is called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), and it's positioned as a slightly diluted or lesser version of the PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which is available on PS5 Pro - the "gold standard" of "AI-guided upscaling", Sony said on the PlayStation blog.
QSSR apparently provides improvements to image detail and "stability", courtesy of "a hand-tuned implementation that maximizes performance on PS5". In a comparison video for Marvel's Wolverine, the close-up image appeared fairly clear - detail is noticeably crisper with QSSR on.
A short comparison video for Ghost of Yotei displayed similar results, revealing less blurry background and environmental detail. "QSSR excels at resolving the fine details in our characters and environments and does so with a level of temporal stability that hasn't been possible on the PS5 console until now," Sucker Punch's lead rendering engineer Jasmin Parry said.
Digital Foundry has already tested QSSR and seems enthusiastic about it, saying that in Marvel's Wolverine's case especially, "the quality boost can be exceptional". "In terms of image quality analysis, suffice it to say that temporal stability is substantially improved, detail level increases, sub-pixel integrity is considerably superior, while artefacts from elements like moving foliage are much reduced. That said, with Ghost of Yotei, a game with already decent image quality saw less dramatic improvements."
The impressive bit about QSSR comes from the PS5 not having dedicated AI upscaling technology like PS5 Pro does, apparently, and Sony finding a way to get it working on PS5 means there's now a potentially better solution for image upscaling than upscalers like FSR - AMD's native solution (PS5 has AMD-based architecture). Nevertheless, DF said: "There remains a big divide between the same game running QSSR on standard PS5 and PSSR on Pro." DF has a QSSR video with comparison footage, if you're interested.
Following QSSR's experimental application in Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei, QSSR is going to be "offered broadly to all PlayStation developers", Sony said in the blog post. It's not clear whether this QSSR update has anything to do with a PS5 firmware update that's just rolled out, incidentally. That update apparently makes some security fixes and improves "system software performance and stability".

item.title: Aion 2's much-awaited worldwide release is days away, following its release in Korea and Taiwan roughly a year ago. Despite this, the MMO has soared - high up Steam's most played game chart. Read more
item.description:
Aion 2's much-awaited worldwide release is days away, following its release in Korea and Taiwan roughly a year ago. Despite this, the MMO has soared - high up Steam's most played game chart.
There are two charts that tell a story. The first is Aion 2 hitting the number-one spot on Steam's Top Sellers list. While Aion 2 is generally a free-to-play game, you currently have to buy your way into early access via a one of a few founders' packs. The cheapest of these packs is £18.49 and it comes with a stack of in-game cosmetics and consumables.
It's through these founders' packs that Aion has outsold other major recent releases. By revenue, Aion 2's founders' packs have made more than EA FC 27, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, and Gears of War: E-Day this week.
As for how many players are actually jumping into Aion 2 early, the Steam Most Played figures paint an interesting picture. As of writing, the game sits at the number nine spot, above Delta Force and Delta Lock, but not quite pushing past big-hitters like PUBG, Apex Legends, and recent multiplayer sensation Wardogs.
This is already an impressive position to be in, but it's of course expected to climb the ranks further once the game becomes open to non-founders a few days from now - and as it becomes free to play.
What is the game like? It's good! I've yet to put enough time into the game to warrant a proper piece of critique on Aion 2, but having messed around with the character creator I was able to make a tiny freaky man last night and thrust him through the main story. Being able to fly around, collect pets through killing enemies out in the world, and build up a character is a lot of fun.
The game is a typical MMORPG with some interesting twists and quirks that sets it apart from its peers. The combat lies between the traditional tab-target approach and a more action-oriented focus you'd see from Black Desert Online. There are plenty of collectables to gather, over 1,100 achievements to collect, and a mix of PvP and PvE events.
Eurogamer reviewed the original Aion in 2009, in which Oli Welsh came away impressed by what was an incredibly popular Korean MMO back in the day. With this game attempting to carry that legacy, forward, why not give it a read?

item.title: James Bond game 007 First Light is getting free DLC today in an Extended Operations update. This adds much-asked-for features to the game - such as New Game Plus, a new harder difficulty mode, a photo mode - as well as more TacSim mission challenges and a couple of game adjustments Read more
item.description:
James Bond game 007 First Light is getting free DLC today in an Extended Operations update. This adds much-asked-for features to the game - such as New Game Plus, a new harder difficulty mode, a photo mode - as well as more TacSim mission challenges and a couple of game adjustments
Those game adjustments are improved weapon handling "fidelity", a press release says, to give more precision to Bond's movement and weapon behaviour. The other adjustment is enemies are now able to throw you off ledges, rather than this being a move only you can do.
New Game Plus is unlocked once you beat the campaign on any difficulty, and once you unlock it, you'll also unlock the game's new 00 difficulty, which is described as "considerably harder".
"The 00 difficulty mode sharpens combat, stealth, and social encounters alike: enemies react faster to bodies and disturbances, certain guard archetypes are swapped for tougher variants, gadget use is restricted within a guard's line of sight, and combat itself becomes far less forgiving, with two-hit kills, tighter parry and side-step timing, and reduced agency gained in a fight," the press release says.
Meanwhile, the TacSim missions bring the Aston Martin Valhalla back, and challenge you to tear across the Slovakian mountainside in it, at varying times of day, as you try to beat certain timed challenges. You can mount rocket-launchers on the car to help, it seems.
There's also another TacSim challenge that takes Bond back to the luxury Pearl resort in Vietnam. There he gets a new mission to retrieve classified documents from a safe before escaping to a rooftop, apparently the whole villa is in play in this mission, and the villa's interior has been redesigned to allow more opportunities for stealth.
Photo mode, finally, lets you stop the action for a piccy whenever you like - mid-battle if desired - and alter character poses as well as adjust a host of other variables such as lighting, lens adjustments, processing filters and so on.
"This DLC is brought to you as a thank you to all the players who've been with us since the game's release," said game director Dominic Vega (this title appears to be a new development - Vega was a mission director before now) in a trailer accompanying the announcement. "So start the game and go earn the number."
007 First Light was released in May and quickly earned success as one of the best James Bond games in years. "007 First Light is less cerebral and replayable than IO's World of Assassination trilogy, but makes up for it with excellent fistfights and oodles of charm," said Rick Lane in Eurogamer's 007 First Light review.
Since then, the game has sold well, with 007 First Light passing 4m sales in three months, suggesting a sequel may well be in IO Interactive's agenda. However, the studio suffered a significant setback around the same time 007 First Light was released, as Xbox pulled out of a publishing deal for Project Fantasy, an online role-playing game it still appears to be making.

item.description:
The early access launch of Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve kicked off on a down note due to some confusion regarding one of the game's pre-order bonuses. Pre-orders of the flight action game include a copy of 2006's Ace Combat Zero: The Belkan War, but early adopters discovered it was not a standalone product, contrary to what they were lead to believe when they pre-ordered the game.
Unsurprisingly, players - who paid the Deluxe edition price of £75 / $90 to access the game three days early - were unhappy.
The Ace Combat studio has now responded, offering a much-needed clarification as to why The Belkan War is not a standalone game on Steam - when it is on consoles - and outline next steps.
"Ace Combat Zero, is offered as a pre-order bonus. Due to licensing restrictions and platform-related considerations, it cannot currently be released on Steam as a standalone application," the developer wrote on Steam.
"As a result, we have chosen to make Ace Combat Zero available through Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. We apologise for any confusion or frustration caused by our failure to clearly communicate this distribution method in advance."
One of the many frustrating side effects of that decision is that Ace Combat 8 must be installed for Ace Combat Zero: The Belkan War to be playable. It also locks The Belkan War out of its own separate Steam cloud saves and achievements, as it exists under a different game. So, will anything be done to address some of those pain points? The developer's statement offers some hope.
"We have carefully reviewed player feedback regarding this issue and understand the concerns that have been raised. We are currently evaluating possible options, including discussions with our platform partners," the statement continues.
"At this time, we cannot guarantee that any changes will be made. However, we are actively exploring potential solutions and will continue working with relevant partners to address player concerns where possible."
The initial shock hit Ace Combat 8's user review rating on Steam, though it has since recovered. At the time of writing, the rating has moved from Mixed to Mostly Positive. It is likely to get even better as the official, 2nd October launch day arrives, as many of those players will at least be aware of the current situation.

item.title: "Look ma, no face," growls Marcus Fenix as I land a headshot on an Elite Sniper from across the map. The foley, wet with viscera and meat, drips and gloops in my ears. item.description:
"Look ma, no face," growls Marcus Fenix as I land a headshot on an Elite Sniper from across the map. The foley, wet with viscera and meat, drips and gloops in my ears. A nearby Locust roars its outrage, a chainsaw revs up to my left, and there's a big meaty slap of muscle on flesh as a Drone ambushes my right flank and tackles me to the floor. Gears of War is back, alright, and it's like it never left.
I think I'd forgotten how incredible this series was at setpieces. There's a sort-of tidal push and pull to the original trilogy, baiting you forward with well-executed maps with waist-high cover and different configurations of enemies and weapons. They lull you into a false sense of security, before something big happens and you're forced out of your comfort zone - the train battle at the end of the first game, the sinking of Jacinto in Gears 2, the 'Mad World' moment in Gears 3, and even the Hamilton-inspired theatre section in Gears 5 all spring to mind. Gears of War: E-Day, I'm pleased to say, continues this legacy with aplomb - and it gets going pretty much straight away.
I'll take a second here to do some housekeeping: this is not a scored review because the access I've been given so far only allowed me to play the campaign locally. A large - if not majority - part of the Gears experience is in online co-op, PvP, and Horde (in fact, I know a lot of people pick these games up for Horde alone). I will continue to play the game in the coming week, and publish another, scored piece later that reflects the whole package. From here on out, it's all campaign.
Given the uber-macho 'ooh-rah' testosterone on display in the series, a casual observer would be forgiven for thinking that's all there is to it: big men with big guns splitting things in half like they're compensating for something. And maybe that was true 20 years ago, but I think Gears has grown into itself with self-awareness, and now feels more akin to something like Starship Troopers or even Robocop; a sly little pastiche of the very things they're celebrating. You can pick that up from the early hours of E-Day, where a sad Marcus Fenix reunites with long-time compatriot Dom Santiago on the anniversary of a former comrade's passing. It's a surprising moment of vulnerability to kick things off - but I guess we need to see the gooey centre of our meathead heroes if we want to feel like there's something worth protecting.
Almost immediately, the situation is FUBAR. Tunnels start popping up all over the city, and a strange subterranean threat begins emerging - ripping civilians to shreds, taking the military by surprise, and threatening the delicate 'peace' the uber-fascist Coalition of Ordered Governments has just about managed to establish in recent months. Marcus, Dom, a greenhorn private called Reyes, and a combat-weary veteran called Mags form a unit - Delta - and make for a rallying point. Your primary objective is survival, and I must give credit to the scenario planners and writers because from this point on-wards the game never lets up.
I do not understand how you can make a campaign of this length and density so fraught. I am pretty sure my cortisol levels are higher this week than they have been all year, simply because I've been saying 'oh God, oh no' to myself every 10 minutes as I've been working through the campaign. My final time clocked somewhere between 20 and 25 hours, playing on Hardcore (the "intended" difficulty, and appropriately brutal), and giving up on collectibles and side missions about halfway through.
When The Coalition is guiding you through its well-manicured setpieces and bombastic cinematic events, Gears of War E-Day is up there with the series' best - I felt transported back to the original trilogy, but with even better combat mechanics underpinning the whole experience. But, sadly, this breakneck pace and tight design work is undercut with open-ended sections that completely hobble to momentum, intentionality, and tension the rest of the game is so good at building up. What's worse is that some of these sections just have you exploring the same section of the city, just in various states of disrepair. If the more streamlined sections are a totem of Gears' best, these languid, free-form bits are emblematic of its worst; evoking some of the weaker pacing in Gears 4 and the more barren reaches of Gears 5. I appreciate the need for a bit of contrast - some downtime to make sure it hurts even more when your face is pushed back against the grindstone - but I think the earlier open bits of E-Day over-correct somewhat, to the detriment of the overall game.
It's hard to stay mad when there are such incredible, fun gauntlets of misery waiting for you around every bend, though. E-Day is canny with how it feeds you toys: you don't get the best weapon in the series - the Torque Bow - until the latter half of the campaign. It's still one of the best weapons to use, maybe in all of gaming. Watching the slowly erecting guideline of tension rise as the explosive bolt you're harbouring gets ready to shunt off with a satisfying ker-chunk… it's bliss. All your favourites are back: the shotgun Gnasher, the sniper Longshot, the heavy Boomshot, and of course the chainsaw-equipped Lancer. At first, I thought the shooting was a bit pants - a little messy, too much recoil, not enough focus or impact.
But then I started getting the upgrades. Each weapon has four slots and you'll need to sniff out lockboxes or do side missions to get more augmentations or unlock more slots. These can focus fire, improve range, enhance lethality, or change the behaviour of your perfect reloads. This is where E-Day stands head and shoulders above past Gears games: each weapon gets a gimmick, and various actions can also grant you a perfect reload in the right circumstances (getting a chainsaw Lancer kill can give you a full clip of powerful ammo, for example). This helps you get into a lethal rhythm: the power fantasy of exploding head after head, nailing a perfect reload every time, and seeing the parabolic increase in your own stopping power. It's enough to make you want a cigarette and a lie down.
I played through most of the game with a Longshot with a scope (perfect for popping heads at range) and a Locust-made Incinerator - which is basically a shotgun filled with acid. The long-range/short-range interplay is good enough to carry all 20+ hours, complemented by some nice mid-range gunplay when you run out of ammo and need to start scavenging dropped guns from the battlefield floor. As a teenager, I never thought of Halo when I was playing Gears, but I couldn't get it out of my head during E-Day. Maybe that's because I only recently wrapped up a LASO run on Halo: Combat Evolved, or maybe it's because the encounter design in this game is top-notch, and demonstrates an intimate understanding of the tools at your disposal, the strengths and weaknesses of each enemy, and the pros and cons of Gears' innate identity as a cover shooter. If you boil it down, every fight is simply 'stay in cover and kill stuff'. But there's a gleeful abandon to it all in E-Day, a willingness to experiment and remix and not patronise you as a player. It instills in you a kind of mania, I think: there are multiple occasions I felt like a berserker during the campaign - intoxicated by a bloodlust and aggression I didn't know I was capable of. Gears!
This forward momentum was only undercut by a few occasional gripes - the aforementioned arrhythmia from the curated and open world sections, and some of the encounters that seemed tuned a little too frustratingly for me (and I like my games hard). There's one fight with two Flayers in a cathedral that had me pulling my hair out - one-shot kills, mixed with some funky camera-work and ungenerous checkpointing, ended up ruining an otherwise excellent little skirmish. This wasn't the only time I butted heads with controls, either. They're mostly fine, but when things get very hectic in the middle of a huge melee, it's easy to glue yourself to the wrong wall, melee at the wrong enemy, die for all the wrong reasons. Between that and getting one-shotted by off-screen enemies, you get a bit of a bad taste in your mouth.
Speaking of which, there is a downside to my praise of the game that's equally worth addressing. I spend a lot of time praising the pacing and narrative above, yet following the latest wave of Microsoft cuts, E-Day's story director Juan Vaca was laid off - this happened just before the launch of the game. Other developers fear they'll be laid off straight after launch - and right before they'd be due their bonuses, too. This does not affect my appraisal of the game and what I've played (actually, it makes me admire the effort that went into it all the more), but I'd be remiss to not add a note here acknowledging the culture, crunch, and context behind the no doubt turbulent journey E-Day has had to this juncture. I wish the developers affected well, and hope they can take some comfort in knowing they made a game that pays homage to - and, in many cases, improves upon - Gears games that have come before.
And ultimately, I think The Coalition has managed to capture some lighting in a bottle with E-Day. It somehow manages to evolve all the best bits of the original 2006-2011 trilogy whilst dropping the cringiest parts of the series. It reevaluates what makes Gears timeless and retrofits the rest, and what emerges is this blood-spattered, muscle-bound colossus that is keenly aware of its strengths and weaknesses. For every gripe, I've got two bits of praise. For every two seconds of frustration I felt, I enjoyed ten seconds of euphoria. Gears has always been a game of contrasts, a winding tension relieved in an explosion of blood and gore - and somehow The Coalition has taken that tempo in micro and expanded it to macro. It's good to have you back, Marcus.
A copy of Gears of War E-Day was provided for this review by Xbox.

CD Projekt Red announced The Witcher 3 the patch's release on social media, noting the following changes:
There are a number of factors seemingly contributing to The Witcher 3 Remastered's apparently increased brightness. A main offender seems to be the Bloom setting, which you can turn off on PC but not on console - perhaps this update addresses that. Graphical flourishes like path tracing and HDR exacerbate the issue.
CD Projekt Red also said it was preparing a hotfix for the PC version relating to a save-game issue, and that it continues "investigating the issues you're reporting via our Technical Support portal". It thanked players for their patience, and for reporting issues they're having.

What's more, it's free to everyone who already owns any version of the game. item.title: PUBG publisher Krafton announced today it is ending development of PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction shooter spin-off announced nearly a year ago. Read more
item.description:
PUBG publisher Krafton announced today it is ending development of PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction shooter spin-off announced nearly a year ago.
Krafton broke the news on Black Budget's Steam page, saying the decision was made following an internal review. "After reviewing the project's development status and future direction, we concluded that its current direction would not allow us to deliver an experience players could enjoy over the long term," Krafton wrote.
"We have therefore made the difficult decision to end development of PUBG: Black Budget. We sincerely thank everyone who took the time to participate in our closed alpha tests and share their feedback."
PUBG: Black Budget, first revealed in November 2025, was positioned as the next major PUBG game, blending extraction shooter elements with those typical of battle royale games. The PvEvP first-person shooter took place on an island trapped in a time loop, and featured strange weather phenomena and other anomalies that were meant to make each match feel different.
Black Budget is now the second PUBG spin-off to have been publicly cancelled. PUBG: Blindspot, the 5v5 top-down tactical shooter that borrowed from Rainbow Six Siege, was cancelled in March after just two months in early access.
Since its reveal, Black Budget hosted several closed tests, with the most recent - and biggest - having taken place in June. The game has seemingly been in development for years; first spotted in a 2023 Krafton financial report, before the publisher announced later that year it was aiming to release the game in the second half of 2024.
It's not clear what the team's next project is going to be, and today's post offers few clues there. "PUBG Studios will carry what we learned from development and testing into future projects, continuing to listen to players as we explore new gameplay experiences," Krafton wrote.
The next PUBG spin-off, PUBG: Ded.Net, was announced at gamescom in August. Developed by Krafton's Madison, Wisconsin studio, Ded.Net is a multiplayer shooter with an 80s aesthetic and roguelite elements, and it's unlike anything else seen in the series so far.

item.description:
Uncharted series developer Naughty Dog is reportedly early in development on a new game in the action-adventure series. That's according to a report from MP1st, which said the game is bringing back series protagonist Nathan Drake in some form, suggesting he may not be the game's lead.
The next Uncharted is also said to be a fresh entry and not a remake of any of the existing games. The project is reportedly being directed by Shaun Escayag, a studio veteran who also directed Uncharted: The Lost Legacy. Noted insider NateTheHate corroborated the report, saying on Resetera that Escayag is indeed working on a new Uncharted game.
Escayag had left Naughty Dog to become creative director of Marvel's Avengers at Crystal Dynamics, but later returned to the studio to work on an unnamed project, which now appears to be this Uncharted game.
The following paragraph includes spoilers for Uncharted 4's ending.
Assuming the game is a continuation of the Uncharted 4: A Thief's End story, one possible way it may go is for Drake and Elena Fisher's daughter, Cassie, who's introduced at the end of the game, to lead this next adventure.
Naughty Dog will reportedly shift to developing the mysterious game after shipping Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, the studio's current main project, which does not yet have a release target. Naughty Dog recently said Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet will be properly revealed in 2027, suggesting it may be released that same year. Given that timeline, we're not likely to see the Uncharted game for quite some time yet.
Beyond a re-release in 2022, the last Uncharted game was 2017's The Lost Legacy, itself an Uncharted 4 spin-off starring some of the same characters.

item.description:
Back in July, new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced a total of 3,200 job cuts across Microsoft's gaming arm, with roughly half of those cuts being made alongside that announcement. The impact was vast. Various developers at Xbox studios, including Activision, Bethesda, Id Software, Blizzard, Mojang, and King suffered layoffs. Double Fine and Compulsion were thrust into independence, while Dishonored 2's Arkane Lyon, State of Decay 3's Undead Labs, and Hellblade's Ninja Theory entered terms for new ownership.
Then, two weeks ago, Xbox made more sweeping cuts. Halo Studios has been drastically reduced in size, with Activision taking control of the sci-fi franchise. Rare and World's Edge were shunted under Activision's umbrella, with the Age of Empires studio reportedly losing roughly half its developers in the process. Obsidian was absorbed by Bethesda, and Ninja Theory entered a consultation process in preparation for a potential closure as its new ownership deal fell through. Undead Labs suffered heavy layoffs as it went independent, while Arkane Lyon is still in a period of consultation with its staff. At least 268 more roles were eliminated in total in that latest round, though it's unclear whether these also include the developers at the likes of Ninja Theory and Undead Labs.
But there's been one Xbox-owned studio left largely off the cutting block so far: Gears of War: E-Day developer The Coalition. Now, following the latest wave of Microsoft cuts - including the sudden departure of E-Day's story director, Juan Vaca - Eurogamer has learned staff at the studio have become increasingly fearful of imminent layoffs, and the potentially major financial consequences which could follow. Eurogamer spoke to multiple sources at the Vancouver-based studio with knowledge of the situation for this article, who have been provided anonymity to protect their identity.
It's worth noting that this sense of trepidation wasn't always the case. Before the latest round of Xbox layoffs, developers at The Coalition had been cautiously optimistic. They believed The Coalition had been spared the cuts, at least thus far, for two main reasons: first, they were working on a big, imminent release for Xbox, in the upcoming Gears of War: E-Day - laying off developers still working on a game would make little sense.
Second, the studio maintains a status as one of Xbox's "good children, so to speak", as one source put it to Eurogamer. The studio's official site, for instance, describes it as "a flagship first-party studio within Xbox Game Studios" and the "home to one of gaming's most critically and commercially acclaimed series" in the long-running Gears of War. Xbox leadership, meanwhile, has largely had a "hands-off" approach to managing the studio over the years, which was, at least for The Coalition, a situation that had seemingly been working well. Those two factors combined to create a sense of relative safety.
Naturally, the knowledge that Xbox still had many job cuts to go still had an impact on morale. Prior gut-punches, such as Tango Gameworks' shock closure after the release of the critically-acclaimed Hi-Fi Rush, were "still on everybody's minds", as one source put it to Eurogamer back in July, shortly after the first stage of Xbox's self-described reset. But the belief continued that it simply wouldn't be smart to "cannibalise" the studio.
Another source had similarly mixed feelings at the time. They felt Microsoft had "faith" in The Coalition, following years of positive support, and that development of Gears of War: E-Day itself was in a good place. But they too felt uneasy, following the first 1,600 job cuts and massive restructuring, describing the mood as "cautious", with the remaining, unspecified layoffs of the 3,200 said to be "hanging over our heads." Energy at the studio was "not full death-march", but at least muted, as they put it, and would likely remain so until three-months after E-Day's release. "The mood is certainly 'let's not celebrate the game until we're three months post launch, just in case', which is very unusual," they said.
Notably, this same source claimed the team had been "crunching hard" in the final months before E-Day's launch, but even then, at the time the atmosphere still wasn't overtly negative. This strenuous push towards the finish line by E-Day developers, for instance, was rewarded with extra vacation time. While the amount given varied from person to person, gestures such as these - despite the crunch - were cited as helping to alleviate worries among staff. Regarding the practice of crunch itself at the studio, Eurogamer understands the internal position is that "extra work" is viewed as occasionally necessary for games such as this, and there is an acknowledgement the team has been working "incredibly hard" on E-Day. The issue of crunch remains a major issue in game development, despite much reporting on the matter and promises of changed culture at various studios over the years.
Ultimately, combined with The Coalition having been largely sheltered from Microsoft's cuts at the time, the sense earlier this summer was that Xbox was "invested" in long-term support in the studio. Cautious optimism remained the ruling sentiment.
That feeling had persisted - until this month. Last week, Gears of War: E-Day's story director Juan Vaca announced he had been laid off as part of Microsoft's cuts, barely two weeks before the game's release. At that time it was unclear how many other developers had been cut. A source speaking to Kotaku claimed a "handful" of developers were also laid off from the studio, shortly before Vaca, for reasons separate from the wider Xbox layoffs. Multiple sources have also told Eurogamer that staff were quietly let go at The Coalition in the past few weeks.
Their departure, along with Vaca's, has taken a hammer to the remaining optimism at the studio. One source described Vaca's departure as "very demoralising". As they put it: "I can only imagine the heartbreak of spending all those years on a game to have the final stretch ripped away, completely out of your control. It's like you planned for a year on a meal for your family where everyone will be there and the day of, you get locked out of the building or something and can't join in."
Coalition developers as a result are "unhappy about it and on edge", they added, "because we honestly expected the layoffs to hit us post-release, but that seems to not matter now. Now we're just expecting the next wave, or being reorganised under Activision or something later this year."
Beyond the stress, meanwhile, Vaca and others' departures have also raised concerns of a financial nature: staff are now concerned that, were they to be laid off within a few weeks of Gears of War: E-Day's release as some fear, they may miss out on potentially lucrative Metacritic bonuses.
The existence of this bonus scheme itself isn't irregular; Metacritic bonuses tied to a game's critical reception have been an established practice at game development studios for years. Likewise the stipulations involved are standard. An internal email, verified by Eurogamer, confirms the existence of this bonus and its relatively typical nature.
However, given the threat of ongoing Xbox cuts, one aspect of this Metacritic bonus has become a cause for concern. In order to be eligible to receive the bonus, developers must be full-time employees at the time of the payout. Studio leadership have communicated to The Coalition developers that this payout date "should be near the end of October", as one source put it.
As a result, it has been unclear to developers still at the studio and who have recently left whether those such as Juan Vaca, who were recently laid off by Xbox and therefore are no longer employed at The Coalition - but will technically still be on payroll at the time of the payout in late October - will receive this bonus if the game hits its targets. Eurogamer understands that despite concerns, those recently impacted, such as Vaca, will still receive their bonuses if the targets are met.
What remains uncertain, however - and crucially so for developers at The Coalition today - is the question of what happens to current staff's bonuses if they are laid off immediately following the release of Gears of War: E-Day as some now fear. As of now, it is still unclear whether these developers would receive their Metacritic bonus.
As a result, a source told Eurogamer that developers being laid off before the Metacritic bonus payout has now become a "morbid joke" among members of the team. The assumption among them, for instance, had been that Vaca would not be receiving his bonus, which could account for tens of thousands of dollars. The possibility of layoffs before the bonus payout has become the "biggest concern" among staff.
Multiple sources have told Eurogamer that the wider actions of Microsoft, in laying off large numbers of staff and cutting multiple studios, has also manifested in a significant amount of scepticism, with some at The Coalition expecting an attempt to "avoid" paying out Metacritic bonuses to any developers hypothetically laid off just before or right after E-Day's release.
Another source said that while those potentially laid off shortly before the payout should technically be eligible for the bonus, they still remained doubtful: "It's hard to believe anything [Microsoft leadership] say anymore after discarding staff in this manner," they explained. Another expressed similar scepticism, saying they "wouldn't put it past Microsoft" to try and avoid paying these bonuses out to any potentially laid off employees.
One more put it like this: "There was a general perception here that we're in a relatively secure spot, despite everything in the industry. But now that feeling is up in the air."
All in all, Xbox's "reset" has, in a matter of months, taken the morale of a strong studio, on the eve of an exciting triple-A release, and turned it sour. With continued cuts planned across Xbox, estimated to still be in the many hundreds at least, time will soon tell whether these fears are unfounded, or if what should be a celebratory milestone for The Colition's developers is spoiled by decisions made far above their heads.
